articles.title: The only town in the U.S. that said yes to data centers
articles.summary: Harwood, North Dakota, may be the only place in the United States that voted in favor of data centers last week. The town, population 845, faced the prospect...
articles.body:
Harwood, North Dakota, may be the only place in the United States that voted in favor of data centers last week.

The town, population 845, faced the prospect of a $3 billion, 1.8-million-square-foot facility on its outskirts.

Resident Michael Swartz hadn't liked the idea. He said he felt city officials had rolled over for a mega-developer who wanted to cash in on the artificial intelligence boom. "It's changing … our small town, and I don't know if it's for the good," he said.

So Swartz, a software engineer, organized to get a measure on the ballot demanding independent reviews and public hearings for big new industrial projects, as well as proposed modifications and expansions of existing ones.

It was one of at least 40 ballot measures in 10 states this election cycle that could have restricted data center development.

On Tuesday, in dozens of cities and towns across the country, voters overwhelmingly endorsed those restrictions. They also elected candidates who campaigned against Big Tech.

Nationally, too, the mood was decidedly anti-data-center. In TV network exit polls, 76 percent of voters said they would oppose the construction of a new data center in their community, and 57 percent (including nearly two-thirds of Democrats) said AI would do more to hurt than to help society.

But confronted with same debate that played out in dozens of other communities, a majority of voters in Harwood were convinced of the merits of data center development. They gave a resounding "no" to increased oversight by a margin of about 3-1.

Harwood residents tend to describe their town as a bedroom community. There's not much there besides a couple of bars and a grain elevator, they say. Many residents commute to work in Fargo, North Dakota's most populous city, and the surrounding metro area.

From the beginning of the data center project, Harwood residents faced the prospect of losing it to their next-door neighbors. Although Texas-based Applied Digital had already contracted 900 acres when the project was announced, Harwood and Fargo disputed who had claim to annex the land.

"It was always going to get built right around the same area that it was now," said Blake Hankey, the mayor of Harwood. "If the data center is going to get put in this similar location, we might as well get the tax benefits and the tax revenue from it."

Hankey estimated that the project would net the town $1.65 million in property taxes once fully completed - about six times the property tax revenue Harwood collected in 2024.

Applied Digital, meanwhile, said it expects the data center to create at least 200 full-time jobs.

The company has also given money to the fire department and to the city for things like a new warming shelter at a local park.

"Proud to be building in Harwood," Jason Zhang, Applied Digital's president, said on social media after Tuesday's ballot measure failed. "Community trust is earned by showing up, listening and following through. Thank you to the people of Harwood for supporting long-term investment in North Dakota."

Mark Kerkvliet, a 40-year resident of Harwood, said he was initially worried that the data center would drive up the costs of power. But talking to officials at the local utility company, a member-owner co-op, assuaged his concerns.

"As soon as I was comfortable with the power use, I was on board," he said. "Not because I like data centers or I like artificial intelligence or anything like that, but because this was very good for the city of Harwood."

He helped organize a door-to-door and mail campaign to counter the ballot initiative, which he was concerned could result in legal action against the town or jeopardize the data center altogether.

Still, Harwood's situation had many characteristics that infuriated communities elsewhere. At contentious council meetings, residents raised questions about environmental impact. They asked about noise. They objected to how the deal had come together.

The mayor signed a nondisclosure agreement when Applied Digital first came to town. And Swartz and other critics complained of a pressure campaign by Applied Digital, with a lawyer for the company weighing in on the prospective text of the ballot measure at a June city council meeting. Swartz eventually rewrote it, using AI.

Eric Sinner, who helped organize the ballot measure, pointed to the example of Janesville, Wisconsin, where he used to live. Janesville was the site of a historic General Motors plant that was decommissioned in the early 2000s, leaving an empty site that would cost the city $35 million to clean up.

"I compare that to what's going to happen to these data centers when they're done," he said. "Who's going to be left with the bill?"

Janesville, coincidentally, was the site of its own referendum after a development company proposed repurposing the GM site into a data center. Residents there passed a measure requiring voters to be consulted on any changes to the old auto plant, adding another obstacle for potential data center construction.

And elsewhere in the U.S., voters let their searing dislike of data centers be known. In Piqua, Ohio, the site of a prospective $1 billion project by Meta, voters approved a ban on large data centers and recalled the officials who had backed the project. Meta said in a statement that it was "proud" of its investments in Ohio and would "work with local officials to determine the future of our investment in Piqua."

Voters in Texas, the location of many major data center projects, elected to the governor's mansion a Democrat, Gina Hinojosa, who has championed a moratorium on new projects.

In response, some large tech companies are emphasizing a more conciliatory approach. OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, said Thursday that it would report how much water its data centers use, halt the use of nondisclosure agreements and commission independent noise studies. (The Washington Post has a content partnership with OpenAI.)

But in Harwood, just 105 voters sided with restrictions on data centers. Another 325 voted not to pass the ballot measure.

"We would have chased what otherwise would be a good neighbor away," Kerkvliet said.

The data center, which broke ground in the fall of 2025, is scheduled to go fully online by the beginning of next year.

articles.title: SpaceX (SPCX) Lands $45 Billion AI Deal As New Contracts Recast Its Growth Story
articles.summary: Space Exploration Technologies (NasdaqGS:SPCX) has secured a reported US$45b AI compute agreement from Anthropic for access to its Colossus and Colossus II d...
articles.body:
Space Exploration Technologies (NasdaqGS:SPCX) has secured a reported US$45b AI compute agreement from Anthropic for access to its Colossus and Colossus II data centers.

Anthropic is expected to pay SpaceX several billions of dollars over multiple years under the Colossus infrastructure arrangement.

Alphabet's Google unit has deepened its partnership with SpaceX and plans to allocate nearly US$1b a month to Nvidia GPU powered AI workloads on SpaceX infrastructure.

The Anthropic Colossus contracts and Google's larger AI workloads highlight only one part of the broader SpaceX investment story. Take a look at 1 major warning sign we have identified for Space Exploration Technologies.

AI infrastructure is drawing capital across a wide set of businesses, so it is worth looking at others with similar exposure through 53 AI infrastructure stocks .

Space Exploration Technologies runs a global satellite broadband network that sits at the intersection of telecom services and large scale data infrastructure, so these AI contracts plug directly into assets already built to move huge volumes of data across borders. For you as an investor, the story links a traditional connectivity business to a growing role as a backbone provider for third party AI workloads.

SpaceX's AI mega deals lean into the bull case, but raise concentration and funding questions

For Space Exploration Technologies, the Anthropic and Google contracts line up squarely with the Narrative that AI demand is carrying much of the upside. They speak directly to the AI segment focus on monetising large Nvidia GPU deployments at Colossus data centers and targeting multi gigawatt compute capacity. That supports the catalyst that global AI workloads are already turning existing infrastructure into higher margin leasing revenue. At the same time, the sheer size of Anthropic's commitments and Google's spend highlights the risk flagged in the Narrative around heavy capex and whether future contract economics and utilisation ultimately justify the billions already directed into Super Intelligence and related projects.

The clearest proof point will be whether future filings and management updates show sustained AI run rate revenue tracking toward the internally referenced US$100b level by late 2026 without a marked deterioration in cash runway or a need for fresh equity that contradicts the current funding assumptions in the story.

articles.title: Here’s the full text of Jensen Huang’s memo to Nvidia
articles.summary: In the memo Nvidia’s CEO acknowledges having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
articles.body: On Sunday, Nvidia announced it was launching an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, an AI executive and agent of the Chinese government. In addition to the Board of Directors announcing the investigation, Huang sent a memo to Nvidia employees acknowledging the affair. You can read the full text below. > To my colleagues at NVIDIA, > I owe my family and all of you an apology. > I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. > Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support. They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it. > To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust. > To my colleagues at NVIDIA, including those I have worked alongside for decades, and to our board, partners, and shareholders around the world: you deserve better from me. Leading NVIDIA is the privilege of my life. My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence. > Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American. > My family bears no responsibility for my choices. I do. Please give them privacy. > — Jensen

articles.title: Anthropic, criadora do Claude, lança IA mais potente e barata | G1
articles.standfirst: Fable 5.2 é o principal lançamento da companhia, que também apresentou uma versão com menos restrições para tarefas de cibersegurança e biologia.
articles.summary: Fable 5.2 é o principal lançamento da companhia, que também apresentou uma versão com menos restrições para tarefas de cibersegurança e biologia.
articles.body:
Ilustração mostra o logotipo da Anthropic e um teclado. — Foto: Dado Ruvic/ Reuters

A Anthropic, empresa americana responsável pelo assistente de inteligência artificial Claude, anunciou nesta segunda-feira (9) uma nova geração de seus modelos de IA. O principal lançamento é o Fable 5.2, descrito pela companhia como uma versão mais potente e mais barata da tecnologia.

O anúncio acontece uma semana antes da provável estreia da empresa na bolsa de valores dos Estados Unidos, em uma oferta que pode transformar a Anthropic na primeira grande desenvolvedora independente de inteligência artificial a abrir capital.

A movimentação ocorre em um momento importante para a companhia, que busca convencer investidores de sua capacidade de competir em um mercado cada vez mais disputado e marcado pela rápida evolução dos sistemas de IA.

Além do Fable 5.2, disponível para todos os usuários, a empresa também apresentou o Mythos 5.2, uma versão com menos restrições para pedidos ligados a áreas como cibersegurança e biologia . O acesso, porém, será limitado inicialmente a um grupo seleto de organizações.

Segundo a empresa, os novos modelos pertencem à família Mythos, considerada sua geração mais avançada de inteligência artificial. A Anthropic afirma que a tecnologia se destaca em tarefas como engenharia de software, análise de dados, pesquisa científica, visão computacional e resolução de problemas complexos.

A companhia também informou que mantém salvaguardas para determinados tipos de solicitações por considerar que modelos dessa categoria podem ser especialmente eficazes na descoberta e exploração de vulnerabilidades em softwares e outras aplicações consideradas sensíveis.

Em apresentações anteriores, a empresa destacou ainda o potencial da tecnologia para aplicações científicas.

Segundo a Anthropic, modelos da linha Mythos foram capazes de auxiliar pesquisas relacionadas ao desenvolvimento de medicamentos, ao design de proteínas e à formulação de hipóteses em biologia molecular que passaram a ser avaliadas por pesquisadores.

A possível chegada da empresa a Wall Street ocorre antes da abertura de capital de sua principal concorrente, a OpenAI, que adiou seus planos para o próximo ano.

A estreia da Anthropic é vista pelo mercado como um importante teste para o apetite dos investidores por empresas que lideram a corrida pelo desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial.

articles.title: De lavador de pratos a bilionário: quem é o CEO da Nvidia envolvido em caso de traição e suspeita de espionagem | G1
articles.standfirst: Jensen Huang fundou a empresa em 1993 e ganhou destaque na corrida pela inteligência artificial. Agora, uma investigação pode colocar em dúvida seu futuro no comando da companhia.
articles.summary: Jensen Huang fundou a empresa em 1993 e ganhou destaque na corrida pela inteligência artificial. Agora, uma investigação pode colocar em dúvida seu futuro no comando da companhia.
articles.body:
O fundador e CEO da Nvidia , Jensen Huang, admitiu ter sido infiel à esposa em meio a suspeitas de que foi alvo de espionagem . No domingo (8), a empresa anunciou uma investigação independente para apurar se ele foi alvo de uma operação de inteligência de outro país.

O executivo começou a vida profissional como lavador de pratos e se tornou um dos dez mais ricos do mundo. Nascido em Taiwan, onde é considerado um herói, Huang migrou para os Estados Unidos e fundou a Nvidia, que se tornou a empresa mais valiosa do mundo.

Agora, o caso pode colocar em dúvida seu futuro no comando da companhia. A investigação ocorre num momento de fortes quedas nas ações da fabricante de chips e de dúvidas entre investidores sobre a sustentabilidade do mercado de inteligência artificial.

Segundo a lista de bilionários da Forbes nesta segunda-feira (9), Jensen Huang aparece como a 8ª pessoa mais rica do mundo, com patrimônio estimado em US$ 162 bilhões (aproximadamente R$ 892 bilhões).

Antes de ganhar destaque na IA, a Nvidia ficou conhecida no mundo dos games. Abaixo, conheça a trajetória de Huang e veja curiosidades sobre a empresa.

Jensen Huang cercado por fãs na Computex, feira de tecnologia que aconteceu em maio, em Taiwan — Foto: Ann Wang/Reuters

O imigrante taiwanês Jen-Hsun Huang, que hoje é conhecido pelo nome Jensen Huang, fundou a Nvidia em 1993, junto de dois sócios. Até 2025, Huang era dono de cerca de 3% da companhia, que se entrou para a bolsa de valores de Nova York em 1999.

Ele passou parte da infância no próprio país e na Tailândia, até que seus pais decidiram enviá-lo com seu irmão para os EUA.

Os dois estudaram em um instituto que funcionava como um reformatório, e Jensen tinha que lavar os banheiros do local, conforme uma reportagem da BBC de 2024.

Aos 15 anos, Huang conseguiu um emprego em uma lanchonete, lavando pratos e servindo mesas . Segundo ele, esta foi uma "excelente" escolha trabalhista.

"Recomendo encarecidamente a todos que tenham seu primeiro emprego no setor de restaurantes, que ensina a ser humilde e trabalhar duro", disse o fundador da Nvidia.

Criança segura cartaz dizendo 'Jensen, eu te amo', do lado de fora de um restaurante onde o fundador da Nvidia jantou, em Taiwan, em maio deste ano — Foto: Ann Wang/Reuters

Huang estudou engenharia elétrica na Universidade Estadual de Oregon e se formou engenheiro em 1984. Ali ele também conheceu a esposa, Lori.

Depois, fez mestrado em Stanford, na Califórnia, e trabalhou em empresas de tecnologia. Em 1993, fundou a Nvidia ao lado de Chris Malachowsky e Curtis Priem.

A ideia surgiu durante um papo deles em uma lanchonete da mesma rede em que Jensen trabalhava lavando pratos.

A Nvidia fabrica chips usados para treinar modelos de inteligência artificial, como o do ChatGPT , que exigem muita capacidade computacional. Entre os clientes da empresa, estão praticamente todas as gigantes da tecnologia, como Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta e Spotify.

Até 2025, a companhia controlava cerca de 80% do mercado de chips de inteligência artificial de ponta, segundo a Reuters.

Seus principais produtos neste setor são as unidades de processamento gráfico (GPU, na sigla em inglês) H100 e A100. A empresa também já lançou o Blackwell (B100), a geração mais avançada, com maior capacidade, desempenho e eficiência, projetada para superar a H100.

A fabricação de chips vai além da inteligência artificial: a Nvidia produz versões para computadores pessoais desses componentes, importantes especialmente para o funcionamento de games . Foi nesse setor, inclusive, que a empresa ficou mundialmente conhecida (saiba mais abaixo) .

Principal produto da Nvidia, o H100, é de longe o chip mais demandado do setor e custa dezenas de milhares de dólares por unidade. Segundo a empresa especializada TrendForce, o ChatGPT requer cerca de 30 mil GPUs (chips) para funcionar.

"Os GPUs são mais difíceis de encontrar do que drogas", ironizou Elon Musk, em um evento organizado pelo "Wall Street Journal" em 2023.

A Nvidia concebe seus processadores, mas não os fabrica em um local próprio , assim como fazem a AMD e a Apple. A maior parte de seus produtos é fabricada pela Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, ou TSMC, referência mundial nesse setor.

E a infraestrutura da IA não seria possível sem centenas de empresas taiwanesas, grandes e pequenas, que fornecem os componentes e o know-how de fabricação necessários para produção dos complexos sistemas de IA da Nvidia.

🎮 Antes de dominar os chips de inteligência artificial, a empresa era completamente dedicada às placas de vídeo , que servem para melhorar a qualidade dos gráficos em jogos e vídeos.

A Nvidia lançou sua primeira GPU em 1999, com o boom da internet, e desenvolveu produtos para "data centers", infraestruturas deslocalizadas que permitem a uma empresa obter uma potência de processamento de dados reservada até então a pesquisadores ou grandes empresas tecnológicas.

As duas principais concorrentes da Nvidia no mercado de placas gráficas são duas empresas americanas: AMD (Advanced Micro Devices) e Intel.

Jensen Huang fala sobre os chips da Nvidia durante a Computex, feira de tecnologia na China — Foto: Ann Wang/Reuters

Os resultados da Nvidia são explicados principalmente pelos altos investimentos de outras companhias em sistemas de inteligência artificial.

A Nvidia é uma das poucas que vende chips usados no treinamento de modelos de IA. A construção desses sistemas depende de milhares de chips como o H100. A Meta, por exemplo, pretendia chegar a 350 mil unidades do componente até o fim de 2024, segundo a Reuters.

O preço de cada H100 não é revelado pela empresa, mas gira entre US$ 16 mil e US$ 100 mil , ainda de acordo com a agência de notícias.

A Huawei e seus pares chineses tentam há anos se igualar à Nvidia na produção de chips de ponta que possam competir com os produtos da empresa norte-americana para modelos de treinamento da IA.

Assim como a AMD, a Nvidia foi proibida de vender seus chips de ponta para a China , ainda no governo de Joe Biden.

Isso faria, teoricamente, com que os rivais asiáticos não pudessem competir com os avanços dos EUA na inteligência artificial.

Mas o lançamento do Deepseek , em janeiro do ano passado, colocou essa ideia em xeque. Em uma semana, a IA chinesa virou o assunto mundial: todos queriam saber como foi possível criar um chatbot que seria semelhante ao ChatGPT, sem os chips da Nvidia e supostamente por um custo muito abaixo.

Segundo reportagem da BBC, o nome da empresa mistura:

NV são as iniciais de "nova/próxima visão" ("new vision", em inglês)

VID é uma referência a vídeo — uma relação com as placas gráficas para computadores que foram o negócio que deu fama à empresa

e o nome também remete à palavra "invidia" , que é usada em latim para se referir à inveja.

Segundo a agência France Press, Huang é um empresário atípico, de modos diretos e aparência descontraída.

Assim como a vestimenta preta usada por Steve Jobs, cofundador da Apple, as roupas de couro que Huang frequentemente usa durante suas apresentações tornaram-se uma marca registrada .

Huang é partidário da "tolerância ao risco" e propenso a que uma empresa "seja suficientemente flexível para mudar de trajetória rapidamente".

Pouco depois do nascimento da Nvidia, o grupo desistiu de um contrato com os fabricantes dos famosos consoles Sega, para se reorientar a um novo processador capaz de competir no mercado de computadores pessoais (PCs). Nessa mudança, a empresa quase faliu, segundo a AFP.

articles.title: Trump Backs Nvidia CEO After He Admits Affair With Suspected Spy
articles.summary: President Donald Trump called Jensen Huang a “fine person” and said he should stay on as the chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp. after the executive admi...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump called Jensen Huang a "fine person" and said he should stay on as the chief executive officer of Nvidia Corp. after the executive admitted having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

"I have not spoken to him about it," Trump told reporters on Sunday before returning to Washington. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on."

Asked whether he should stay on, Trump said, "I think so. Oh yeah, sure."

Nvidia said its board would begin an investigation into whether Huang was a target of a foreign intelligence agency.

Asked if he plans to take Huang on his trip to Asia later this month, Trump said that he doesn't know but would take him along.

"I haven't heard he's done anything wrong," Trump said.

US intelligence officials had told the Trump administration earlier that a woman who had become close to Huang was working for a Chinese spy agency, which recruited her to collect information on him, the New York Times reported Friday. On Sunday, the newspaper reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had overseen the production of a secret memo on US concerns.

articles.title: China may have just solved AI's biggest bottleneck
articles.summary: China plans 5GW of green AI computing capacity as Envision rolls out its new high-voltage power technology
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

China puts its first commercial 800V DC data center power system into operation

Envision converts 10kV grid electricity directly into an 800V DC supply

New power architecture combines solid-state transformers with battery storage for AI facilities

China's Envision claims to have put an integrated 800-volt direct-current power architecture into commercial operation at an AI facility in Inner Mongolia.

The installation is located at the Galaxy AI campus in Ulanqab, where trials of its Dubhe controller and supporting energy model began in August 2026.

The company describes the deployment as the first commercial use of this configuration, although independent performance figures have not yet been disclosed publicly.

A different route from grid electricity to computing hardware

Conventional facilities generally convert incoming electricity through several stages before delivering power suitable for servers and accelerators, adding equipment and potential conversion losses.

Envision's design instead uses a solid-state transformer to convert 10-kilovolt medium-voltage alternating current directly into an 800-volt direct-current distribution line.

The company says this arrangement reduces conversion steps, improves electrical efficiency and allows power equipment to occupy substantially less physical space within data centers .

A higher-voltage distribution network can also reduce the amount of copper required for cabling, potentially lowering material requirements as computing installations expand rapidly.

The architecture includes battery storage intended to respond rapidly when processor demand changes, while also supplying temporary backup during unexpected interruptions.

Envision says the storage system can provide immediate support over seconds and maintain backup capability across periods measured in several minutes.

Its controller coordinates the transformer and batteries within milliseconds, aiming to manage sudden changes in electricity consumption from GPUs .

That coordination matters because AI workloads can cause substantial swings in demand, placing additional pressure on electrical infrastructure supplying densely packed computing equipment.

The company also says its arrangement can accommodate higher-density server racks, allowing operators to install more computing capacity within a given floor area.

Ambitions extend beyond the first installation

Envision's Galaxy facility is expected to grow to 3 gigawatts, with the company saying its eventual capacity could serve one million AI accelerators.

Envision also intends to introduce the technology through Mission Gobi, an initiative seeking 5 gigawatts of renewable-powered computing capacity by 2030.

That programme is focused on desert locations, where the company expects renewable generation and energy storage to support large computing developments.

The system has been designed to work alongside renewable electricity sources, while its batteries are intended to balance supply and changing computing requirements.

However, the company has not provided independently verified measurements quantifying efficiency improvements, installation costs or savings compared with conventional power systems.

The announcement does not also establish how the architecture performs under sustained full-load conditions or across facilities with substantially different hardware configurations.

The deployment therefore marks a commercial milestone for Envision, while the scale of its claimed operational advantages awaits detailed independent evidence.

articles.title: Nvidia CEO’s Affair Admission Counters Past Statements on Ties
articles.summary: For more than a year, Nvidia Corp. minimized the ties that Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang had with Megaspeed, the once-obscure spinoff of a Chinese gam...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- For more than a year, Nvidia Corp. minimized the ties that Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang had with Megaspeed, the once-obscure spinoff of a Chinese gaming enterprise, and a woman named Huang Le who helped set it up.

Both Nvidia and Jensen Huang had characterized Megaspeed as a legitimate, albeit large, buyer of Nvidia's AI chips despite US government concerns that China could be using the Singapore-based firm to gain access to advanced semiconductors. And they'd described reports of Jensen's relationship with Huang Le, who also goes by Alice Huang, as professional in nature.

Just in the past two weeks, despite reports of a close relationship between the two, Jensen defended himself, calling their interactions "completely normal."

Those comments made Jensen Huang's admission that he'd cheated on his wife of more than four decades all the more shocking, contrasting with his and the company's past statements. On Sunday, Nvidia said its board was investigating whether he'd been "the target of a foreign intelligence effort," following reports that US officials suspected Alice Huang was hired by a Chinese spy agency. The revelations have left Jensen Huang's future as the face of the AI infrastructure boom and head of one of the world's most valuable companies hanging in the balance.

Jensen Huang's ties to Alice Huang date as far back as 2024. The New York Times reported in October 2025 that she was mingling with a group of tech executives at a bar in Taipei a year earlier when she bet she could get Jensen to join them. Shortly after Alice Huang reached out, the Times reported, Jensen Huang showed up and took a whiskey shot with the group.

In response to that report, Nvidia spokesman John Rizzo said at the time that the company's "field operations teams often host groups of customers and partners at conferences, and when Jensen is available, may ask him to visit to provide updates on the market."

Nvidia continued to defend its business with Megaspeed, a so-called neocloud that rents out access to computing power for AI workloads, when Bloomberg News reported last December that the US government had been investigating Megaspeed's ownership structure and whether the firm had diverted Nvidia chips to China. Such smuggling would represent a major breach of US curbs aimed at limiting China's AI and military prowess.

articles.title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50” | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nvidia’s board is investigating Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, and Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld thinks it’s roughly a coin flip whether Huang stays on as CEO.
articles.body:
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife. But this isn’t a case of just another CEO having an extramarital affair. The romantic interest is Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy who was feeding information back to Beijing. In short, the stakes reach well beyond Nvidia, given how many tech and financial partners depend on its place at the center of the AI economy. “I’m responsible for an entire industry ,” Huang recently told Bloomberg in a sit-down.

A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Washington dismissed the allegations in late October as “ groundless smears and slanders ,” and no one has been charged. But U.S. intelligence officials reportedly briefed President Donald Trump about their concerns a year ago, and unnamed senior officials inside the Trump administration told the Times that they doubt Huang could have remained unaware all that time of Alice Huang’s intelligence-gathering role for China. When Trump was first briefed, the Times reported, officials didn’t believe Huang knew, and it isn’t clear whether their assessment has changed. The board, meanwhile, says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised.

The question is whether Huang can survive this. To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits. Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.

First, the damage. Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted. But he called this episode “remarkably poor judgment.” Even if Huang was merely naive, he said, “any employee in Nvidia other than him would be fired over this,” and the recklessness alone would mean “an irretrievable loss of confidence.”

Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped. The term comes from Edwin Hollander, a social psychologist who proposed in a 1958 paper that people earn latitude in a group by showing competence and following its rules. Huang has been earning latitude since he co-founded Nvidia in 1993. But all that goodwill can run out when a screw-up looks self-serving or touches the group’s core norms. Here that group includes Nvidia’s board, its roughly 42,000 employees who are bound by security rules, and, in a looser sense, the U.S. government, given it restricts its exports.

We also talked about precedents, except, as it turns out, there really are none for what’s unfolding right now. Executives who survive personal scandals sometimes pick up where they left off at another company, Sonnenfeld observed. Former HP CEO Mark Hurd is one example. Between 2005 and 2010, he drove HP to the top of the tech industry by revenue, then was pressured to resign after he filed inaccurate expense reports that hid a personal relationship with a contractor. Oracle hired him about a month later. Huang has no equivalent because Nvidia is his company

As for the bench at Nvidia, that doesn’t really exist either. While there is typically a hierarchy inside companies of Nvidia’s scale and importance, Huang has kept things as flat as possible, with about 60 direct reports by his own account. That structure makes it hard to figure out who would succeed him (though his children, both of whom work at Nvidia, are sometimes the subject of succession speculation ). That won’t stop the worldwide guessing game that’s sure to follow. And boards in crisis often reach for a “messianic solution” from outside, Sonnenfeld said, floating former Google CEO Eric Schmidt as one idea.

Nvidia’s role at the center of a massive and complex circular financing web is what makes this particular predicament so tricky and, undoubtedly, terrifying for a wide number of constituents. Nvidia isn’t just the biggest provider of chips driving the AI boom but also largely the bank behind the buildout. In addition to stakes in hundreds of smaller startups, Nvidia has invested in OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, CoreWeave and Nebius. In August, it also signed preliminary agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion over time, and Huang has said Nvidia could backstop up to a quarter of it. The move was widely interpreted as a way to spread risk. Still, a leadership crisis at the center is how a stumble becomes a collapse.

So what’s Nvidia’s board likely doing right now? Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, whose company Nvidia has backed, had a lot to say about selling chips to China at Davos back in January, likening it to “ selling nuclear weapons to North Korea .”

Now the board’s independent members — meaning everyone but Huang — will have to establish what technology reached China if any, and by what routes, including by better understanding Nvidia’s relationship with Megaspeed. The Singapore cloud company, which grew out of a Chinese gaming business and became Nvidia’s largest buyer in Southeast Asia, bought roughly $2 billion of its chips , the New York Times reported in October 2025, raising broader questions about whether it was helping China circumvent U.S. export restrictions by re-exporting the chips to China or renting them to Chinese customers remotely. (An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill after the Times report that the allegations were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year .”)

In the meantime, Huang will keep running the company, Nvidia said Sunday. That’ll be a tall order, even for a CEO who already spends much of his time traveling the world to promote Nvidia. For starters, three House chairmen want a closed-door briefing from Huang on November 18. Nvidia is also reporting its newest earnings on November 17. Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.

Only one thing is certain right now. Huang doesn’t own the kind of super-voting stock that would cement his power at Nvidia. Sonnenfeld often argues for dual-class structures that empower founders, and he says Huang’s success without one has been the best counterargument to that case. But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.

This episode may be remembered as a pivotal moment for how the tech industry guards its secrets. Sonnenfeld argues tech has been “way too lax” compared with defense contractors that face clearance regimes. The arrest last month of an OpenAI engineer points to the same problem. He was accused of hiding a recording device behind a TV in an executive conference room, and while OpenAI has said it has no indication that model weights, source code, or customer data were accessed, the case highlights how exposed tech companies are to people who get close.

Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone). The bigger test comes when Nvidia’s employees, customers and partners, and, indirectly, the millions of Americans with Nvidia in their 401(k) plans, have to decide whether an AI economy built largely on the judgment of Huang still makes sense.

articles.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says he does not want his son to have an AI chatbot as his best friend; reveals why children need greater protection from AI
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has expressed reservations about children developing relationships with artificial intelligence chatbots, saying he does not want
articles.body: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has expressed reservations about children developing relationships with artificial intelligence chatbots, saying he does not want his son to have an AI bot as his best friend. He made that particular remark during a US Senate hearing in May 2025. More recently, in an exclusive interview with Vanity Fair, published on October 5, 2026, Altman discussed raising children in a world increasingly shaped by AI and said he had not decided at what age he would allow his own children to use ChatGPT. He also voiced concerns about excessive technology use during childhood and the potential effects of emerging technologies on developing brains. His comments come amid growing concerns among child development experts about AI companions, emotional dependence and children's ability to build meaningful human relationships.Why Sam Altman is cautious about introducing AI to his childrenSpeaking to Vanity Fair, Altman said he had not settled on an appropriate age for his children to start using ChatGPT. He indicated that he was not comfortable introducing the technology to them at their current age.The OpenAI chief also expressed support for limiting children's exposure to technology more broadly. He believes young children should have opportunities to spend time outdoors, play in nature and experience the world beyond screens.Altman raised concerns about children becoming accustomed to touchscreens and short-form videos at an early age. He also pointed to the uncertainty surrounding the effects of emerging technologies on developing brains.He acknowledged that children growing up today would inevitably encounter AI and would need to understand how to use it. However, he questioned whether introducing conversational AI during early childhood was necessary, particularly when its long-term effects on development are still being studied.What Sam Altman said about AI becoming a child's best friendAltman had addressed the question of AI companionship during a US Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation hearing on May 8, 2025.During the hearing, Senator Bernie Moreno referred to Altman's experience as a new father and asked whether he wanted his child's best friend to be an AI bot. Altman responded directly: "I do not."He subsequently explained that children needed a much higher level of protection when interacting with AI services than adult users. He said OpenAI wanted to give adults considerable freedom in using its products while applying stricter rules and safeguards for younger users.Altman also acknowledged the difficulty of reliably determining whether an online user is a child or an adult. He said that if technology companies could identify users' ages with greater certainty, they could offer adults more flexibility while maintaining tighter restrictions for children.During the same discussion, he raised concerns about people increasingly turning to AI systems for life advice and emotional support. He described the development as relatively new and said it needed to be understood and monitored carefully.Experts are concerned about children forming emotional bonds with AIThe growing popularity of AI companion applications has prompted warnings from child welfare organisations and psychological experts. Unlike conventional search engines or digital assistants, AI companions are designed to maintain conversations, respond to personal information and simulate relationships.This can make interactions feel like conversations with friends, mentors or confidants. However, the responses are generated by AI systems rather than people with genuine emotions or personal experiences.In June 2025, the American Psychological Association (APA) published its health advisory, Artificial Intelligence and Adolescent Well-being. It highlighted concerns about adolescents developing unhealthy relationships with chatbots and warned that young users may be less likely than adults to question the accuracy and intentions of information provided by AI systems.The advisory also warned that adolescents may struggle to distinguish simulated empathy from genuine human understanding. Strong attachments to AI characters could interfere with the development of real-world relationships and social skills.The APA recommended age-appropriate privacy settings, interaction limits, transparency about AI-generated responses and human oversight. It also called for developers to establish clear boundaries around simulated human relationships to prevent AI systems from undermining real-world connections.The organisation acknowledged that AI can support young people through educational and creative activities, including brainstorming, summarising and understanding information. However, it emphasised the need to make children aware of the technology's limitations.Nearly three in four teenagers have used AI companions, study findsResearch published by Common Sense Media on July 16, 2025, highlighted how widely AI companions had spread among teenagers in the United States.Its report, Talk, Trust, and Trade-Offs: How and Why Teens Use AI Companions, surveyed 1,060 US teenagers aged 13 to 17 in April and May 2025. It found that 72% had used AI companions, while 52% said they used them at least a few times a month. Around 33% reported using these platforms for social interaction and relationships.Among teenagers who had used AI companions, 33% said they had chosen to discuss important or serious matters with an AI companion instead of a real person. The survey also found that 24% of AI companion users had shared personal or private information, such as their real name, location or personal secrets, with these platforms.The research also offered a more nuanced picture of teenagers' relationships with AI. Despite widespread adoption, 80% of teenagers who had used AI companions said they spent more time with real-life friends than with AI companions. Additionally, 67% found conversations with AI less satisfying than conversations with their real-life friends.The findings suggest that although AI companions are becoming part of teenagers' social experiences, many young users continue to value human friendships more highly.What UNICEF says about protecting children from AI companionsUNICEF has also highlighted the risks associated with AI systems designed to act as friends or emotional companions.In a July 2025 article published by UNICEF Innocenti, titled The Risky New World of Tech's Friendliest Bots, researchers highlighted concerns about children's growing use of AI companions. The article featured research and an interview with digital innovation specialist Samia Firmino, examining the potential effects of these platforms on young users.It raised concerns about inadequate safety protections, inappropriate chatbot responses and the possibility of children developing unhealthy attachments to artificial companions.UNICEF subsequently updated its Guidance on AI and Children in December 2025. The third version included specific recommendations addressing AI companions and their potential impact on children's rights and well-being.The guidance calls on governments and technology companies to prioritise children's safety, protect their personal information, ensure transparency and establish accountability for AI systems. It also emphasises the importance of designing technology around children's developmental needs and preparing them to use AI responsibly.UNICEF recognises that AI can provide educational opportunities and improve accessibility for children, including those with disabilities. However, it stresses that these benefits must be balanced against the risks associated with children's interactions with increasingly sophisticated AI systems.You use AI every day. articles.body:
Nov 9 (Reuters) - Nvidia's board is probing whether CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, following a media report alleging that he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.

Here are comments by analysts ‌and prominent figures:

RYU YOUNG-HO, SENIOR ANALYST AT NH INVESTMENT & SECURITIES:

"It appears the US government had been aware of the matter involving Jensen Huang ‌for several months, so the immediate impact is unlikely to be significant.

"The biggest potential risk for South Korean companies would be if a prolonged investigation or internal review were to lead Nvidia ​to delay its investment decisions.

"If Nvidia's product shipments or launches were to be delayed, it could have broader implications for the semiconductor industry."

GARY BLACK, TESLA INVESTOR WHO MANAGES MONEY FOR THE FUTURE FUND LLC:

"I doubt Jensen Huang will be able to remain as (Nvidia) CEO. This could put short-term pressure on the stock of the second most valuable company in the world.

"He has no natural successor within the company. While Huang has not committed any crime or tort, his code of conduct and ‌judgment will be called into question, which will likely ⁠result in his removal ...

"Many portfolio managers will reduce their (Nvidia) holdings in the coming weeks as a result of uncertainty over who could succeed Jensen."

"I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he's a fine person, ⁠but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine ... I think he's an honourable guy."

"I am not suggesting he gets a free pass. If indeed this is more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem. I like the guy. He has done a lot of good for ​the ​world and I hope the damage here is minimal. That is, I am hoping ​for a simple affair, not a risk to our national ‌security."

"While Nvidia has sought to reassure us all, there are several layers here, beginning with the unfortunate timing.

"For example: The company is systemically important for tech, markets and the economy; Investors tend to struggle to price in key-person and governance issues; and there are fluid national security and geopolitical dynamics."

articles.title: Kainos CEO Brendan Mooney says government 'cautious' on AI deployment
articles.summary: Brendan Mooney was speaking as Kainos announced a record half-year performance.
articles.body:
The chief executive of Northern Ireland's largest software firm has said UK government clients remain cautious about the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Brendan Mooney was speaking as Kainos announced a record half-year performance with a pre-tax profit of £36m on sales of £269m.

The company recently won a £111m "digital borders" contract with the Home Office to be delivered over the next four years.

Mooney said there were "parallel conversations" on AI with "buzz and excitement" about its capabilities on one hand and the reality of deploying it in large organisations on the other.

He told BBC News NI: "The hardest thing we do as a company is to get an AI system live and to keep it live because an AI system runs on top of a model, that model drifts, either through changes to the model or changes to how the model interprets the data."

He said that clients operating in regulated or sensitive areas like healthcare or defence are "super cautious" about how AI will be used in their organisations.

Mooney said that Kainos' internal spending on AI has doubled in the last year partly due to greater use across the business as well as an increase in the prices charged by the major AI firms.

He added that the productivity gains from using in AI in software development has been "well proven" and is generating value for the business.

Those productivity gains have led to concerns that AI is costing jobs across a variety of professions such as software development and business consulting.

Mooney rejected as "one-dimensional" the view that AI tools could replace the need for junior staff.

He said that while, historically, graduates were asked to do simple tasks, they can - and should - be asked to do more complex work.

"Yes, they need time to build their skills and knowledge, and judgement is ever-increasingly an important part of what we do today.

"But I just think it shows limited imagination if you're saying that all graduates are good for is doing something very simple."

He expects more than 200 people to join the business this year through graduate and school-leaver programmes which he called "our strongest ever graduate intake".

The company currently employs almost 4,000 people across its global operations with almost 1,400 of them in Northern Ireland.

It is currently developing a new HQ building in the centre of Belfast.

articles.title: Nvidia stock falls after investigation into CEO, bucking market rally
articles.summary: Wall Street rallied sharply on Monday, despite a 5% decline in Nvidia shares, as markets continued to rebound from last week’s sharp tech sell-off.
articles.body: Wall Street rallied sharply on Monday, despite a 5% decline in Nvidia shares, as markets continued to rebound from last week’s sharp tech sell-off. The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq surged to start the week, buoyed by gains in shares across sectors, from tech to industrials. The Nasdaq soared 3%, set for its best day in months. Meanwhile, Nvidia shares dropped, extending a recent bout of weakness, after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair and the company said it was investigating reports he was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort.” The developments come at a rocky moment for the AI boom, with volatility rising in recent weeks over concerns about the sustainability of the data center buildout. Nvidia shares (NVDA) are down more than 20% from their peak a month ago and last week erased their gains for this year. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite on Thursday closed in correction, down more than 10% from its peak one month ago. Nvidia, which makes semiconductor chips, has been at the heart of the AI bull market over the past four years. Huang has been one of AI’s main cheerleaders, with enormous influence over Wall Street’s outlook for the boom. The investigation into Huang and allegations of a foreign intelligence effort raise serious questions for the company at the center of the buildout with deals across major tech companies and adds to heightened tensions between the United States and China. “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information,” Nvidia said in a statement Sunday. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” Huang said in a separate note to Nvidia staff. The key questions for investors are whether the board’s investigation will uncover anything more serious that could jeopardize Huang’s role as CEO as well as potential regulatory implications that could constrain sales, analysts at Citi wrote in a note. The heightened uncertainty comes after the Democrat sweep in the midterm elections is forcing investors to reckon with the risk of a slowdown to the data center buildout. Tech stocks in recent weeks had already tumbled over nerves about massive AI spending and demands to see more returns on investment. Investors are on edge about the AI boom, and volatility in Nvidia can add to the jitters. Star of the AI boom Huang founded Nvidia in 1993, took the company public in 1999 and presided over its transition into being a central pillar of the AI boom. Nvidia pioneered graphics processing units, which are semiconductor chips. The company’s chips were built to innovate in the gaming industry, providing enhanced computing power and visuals. By the 2010s, researchers began to use the powerful chips for budding AI technology. Nvidia in 2016 delivered a supercomputer powered by its chips to OpenAI, which launched ChatGPT to the public in 2022. The company positioned itself as the core provider of GPUs for tech companies, and its stock has skyrocketed alongside the AI boom, lifting the broader stock market to record highs. Nvidia shares are up 1,250% over the past four years, since the month OpenAI first released ChatGPT to the public. Nvidia last year became the first company in the world to surpass $5 trillion in market value, and it accounts for roughly 7% of the S&P 500. Nvidia’s chips are used across the industry to power AI models, from Anthropic’s Claude to Meta’s Muse. The company has also emerged as a key player in backing massive infrastructure deals for the AI buildout. Nvidia’s earnings reports have become known as investors’ Super Bowl, and comments from Huang have ignited major market moves in recent years. The CEO, known for his bold vision and unique style, has also been championed by retail investors. His importance for the company and the stock is raising the stakes over uncertainty about the investigation. “Jensen is the core DNA of Nvidia and its AI success and ambitions are heavily tied to him staying on as CEO,” Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., wrote in a note. “Jensen is not replaceable,” Ives added. But investors are still discerning whether the personal crisis will have significant impacts on the company’s outlook, and are waiting to see whether the board’s investigation will glean any further critical insights for the company and AI boom. The broader market rallied sharply on Monday despite Nvidia’s decline. “This is, for now at least, a personal scandal,” Nigel Green, CEO at deVere Group, wrote in a note. “If the probe finds anything more serious, the selloff could deepen, so investors need to weigh these risks carefully,” Green added. Nvidia’s stock had been losing some luster this year, lagging behind other chipmakers like Micron Technology (MU) and Marvell Technology (MRVL). But that’s only after Nvidia posted enormous returns in recent years. The company remains a central part of the AI boom, and the Huang investigation is just one more factor for investors to weigh. Keeping an eye on the stock is critical for gauging the outlook for the broader market. “Jensen is much more than just a CEO — like Elon Musk, he is the face of the firm,” David Rosenberg, founder and president at Rosenberg Research, wrote in a Monday note. “It would not be a stretch to suggest that this is the deepest crisis the chip giant has found itself in during its three-decade history,” Rosenberg wrote. Nvidia is expected to report quarterly earnings on November 17. “Nvidia is huge and at the heart of the AI supply chain, so what happens to this stock matters to the rest of the market,” Neil Wilson, a strategist at Saxo Markets, wrote in a note.

articles.title: Trump’s 60 Minutes interview touched on AI safety, threat to arrest an AI exec
articles.summary: In a 60 Minutes interview, Trump said the DOJ is managing AI safety risks and claimed China has “no guardrails.”
articles.body: Asked about AI executives’ warnings about their models’ safety on 60 Minutes, Trump said, “I think that the risk is not nearly as real as it– as they talk, and I think the risk can be managed, and it’s managed.” He claimed the DOJ is managing that risk, saying, “We had a situation where somebody was reported to us to be doing something bad with AI. We called them very strongly and said, ‘Get ready to go to jail. Please give your wife a kiss good night.’” Trump refused to name the person or company he was referring to, but said it was the leader of an AI company, “One of the big ones.” He claimed that after the threat of arrest, “this person totally changed everything.” Despite previously claiming that “artificial intelligence” is a term used by people he considers the enemy, Trump said AI rather than SI or super intelligence multiple times during the interview. Eventually he said China’s Xi is “…all in to SI, as I call it, because it really is super intelligence. It’s a much better name, I think, because it’s not artificial.” 60 Minutes’s Ross Douthat went on to ask if Trump would work with Democrats on AI safety, and Trump said he “absolutely would,” adding, “I don’t mind guardrails, but I don’t want to put us in a deep second position. We’re leading number one. And China has no guardrails, by the way. [...] They have the guardrails that whatever President Xi says goes. With me, it’s pretty strong, but it’s not quite that strong.”

articles.title: Days before he got an offer from Meta, to lead the company's AI lab, Alexandr Wang sent Mark Zuckerberg a 'long note' whose first principle was that he does not need a lot of people, as what matters  is ...
articles.summary: Days before accepting an offer to lead Meta’s artificial intelligence efforts, Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang sent Mark Zuckerberg a lengthy memo outlining
articles.body: Days before accepting an offer to lead Meta’s artificial intelligence efforts, Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang sent Mark Zuckerberg a lengthy memo outlining how he would approach the company’s AI ambitions. According to a Fortune report, the first principle in that note was simple: success in AI is not about having the largest workforce, but about having the highest concentration of top talent. Wang, the 29-year-old co-founder of Scale AI who now heads Meta Superintelligence Labs, revealed details of the memo during an appearance alongside Zuckerberg on the Cheeky Pint podcast hosted by Stripe co-founder John Collison. The discussion offered a rare glimpse into the conversations that preceded one of the biggest executive hires in the AI industry.A 44-minute call that led to a major hireThe partnership began taking shape in April 2025, shortly after Meta’s Llama 4 models received a lukewarm response. Wang recalled receiving a WhatsApp message from Zuckerberg asking whether he had time for a call. That conversation lasted about 44 minutes.Two days later, Wang sent Zuckerberg a detailed memo describing what he would do if he were running Meta’s AI division. Recalling the advice, Zuckerberg said the very first principle centred on “talent density.” “The very first thing is that you don’t need a lot of people, and talent density is the thing that matters,” Zuckerberg said. According to the Meta CEO, the second principle was being willing to rebuild from scratch. Zuckerberg acknowledged that the company was unhappy with the direction of Llama 4 and was prepared to reorganise its AI efforts if necessary.Why Mark Zuckerberg chose Alexandr WangThe decision to put Wang in charge of Meta’s AI ambitions surprised some observers because the entrepreneur had built Scale AI into a data-labelling giant but had never personally led the training of a frontier AI model. Zuckerberg, however, said he had admired Wang for years and viewed him as one of the sharpest entrepreneurs of his generation. Before making the decision, he spoke with leaders across major AI research labs but remained convinced that Wang was the right person for the role. “I talked to like all the leaders of all the labs, like all the heads of research,” Zuckerberg said on the podcast. “And I was like, no, Alex is the guy.”A ‘supernova’ recruiting pushZuckerberg described what followed as a “supernova” recruiting effort. Meta paid $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Scale AI to bring Wang aboard and reportedly offered $100 million pay packages to OpenAI researchers. Zuckerberg cleared his calendar for two months, and he said neither of them slept much in the first couple of months. Meta’s core research team in the lab has fewer than 200 people, and Wang said it is closer to 100. It is backed by larger infrastructure and product teams at a company of about 75,000 employees. Wang said he built a culture of “insecure overachievers.”The results and the stakesThe lab’s first model, Muse Spark, arrived in April. On Monday, Meta released Muse Wonder, the first model from the lab it calls frontier-class. Wang said it is state-of-the-art on his team’s measurements for personal and professional agent tasks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the flagship version lands roughly level with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic but a couple of points behind the leader, according to AI Weekly.The Muse app launched in the US on September 8 and quickly became the most popular free app in Apple’s App Store. It topped 2.5 million downloads in about two weeks, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNN. Zuckerberg said late last year that Meta was discussing spending as much as $100 billion or $200 billion, and recalled asking Wang whether he was sure it would work. Wang said Meta CFO Susan Li pulled him aside at an executive gathering in Hawaii to stress that the model has to work, because failure would be very bad in financial terms. Meta expects 2026 capital spending of $130 billion to $145 billion, nearly double last year’s $72.2 billion.Wang also praised Zuckerberg’s leadership, saying he has fully internalised power laws. Once Zuckerberg adopts a belief, Wang said, the speed and scale at which he will change earlier decisions are unusual.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Anthropic joins AI’s natural gas frenzy, buys $3.4B worth of turbines
articles.summary: Anthropic bought billions of dollars' worth of natural gas turbines in a deal that could give it buyer's remorse.
articles.body:
AI's power crunch has become so acute that Anthropic, a company that has generally avoided buying physical infrastructure, is spending $3.4 billion on natural gas turbines.

The AI company, which is planning to go public this year, is buying Caterpillar generators that equipment supplier OnePWR had originally ordered, according to a Financial Times report . The generators are capable of producing up to 1.7 gigawatts of electricity.

Historically, Anthropic has preferred to rent rather than buy. The company disclosed in its S-1 filing in May that it is paying SpaceX subsidiary xAI $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 to use xAI's computing power.

"We expect to enter into additional similar services contracts," Anthropic stated in the filing, meaning more deals to rent computing power.

But as demand for compute ramps up, the market for power has also grown increasingly uncertain, which may have forced its hand. The backlog for natural gas turbines stretches into the early 2030s, and queues to connect to the electrical grid can be just as long.

Anthropic's purchase looks like a last resort.

According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago but couldn't find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer.

It's not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic's apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up.

AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google , Amazon , Microsoft , and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on-site, rather than drawing from the public grid.

The binge has given a second wind to fracking , the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, Anthropic might have a serious case of buyer's remorse.

According to the report, OnePWR ordered the turbines a couple years ago but couldn’t find financing to complete the purchase. Anthropic had planned to buy them from OnePWR but instead went directly to Caterpillar, the manufacturer.

It’s not clear why OnePWR was unable to secure financing despite Anthropic’s apparent interest as a customer. Whatever the case, Anthropic likely wanted to keep the generating capacity to itself rather than give a competitor an opportunity to snap it up.

AI companies have been ramping up their purchases of natural gas equipment and supplies in recent years. Google , Amazon , Microsoft , and Meta have all announced plans to build massive natural gas power plants to power their data centers on-site, rather than drawing from the public grid.

The binge has given a second wind to fracking , the drilling method used to extract natural gas from underground rock. And if the buildout proceeds as planned, U.S. data centers alone could consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined by 2035. The reliance on natural gas also exposes hyperscalers to price fluctuations. One analyst expects that prices could more than triple by the end of the decade in some markets. If that happens, Anthropic might have a serious case of buyer’s remorse.

articles.title: The future of AI hinges on… Jensen Huang’s sex life?
articles.summary: NVIDIOT.
articles.body: I would prefer that these people’s sex lives were none of my business but I guess we have to talk about Jensen Huang and the National Security Incident. Who could have guessed that the guy who was out here signing titties might not have great judgment about how to behave around women? Alice Huang — no relation to Jensen — is a former TV reporter. That was before she became “an executive” at Megaspeed, which bought $4.8 billion of hard-to-get Nvidia chips, starting around the time she was being photographed with Jensen in a Taipei bar in 2024. “To many in the industry, the well-funded push by Megaspeed into A.I. appeared to come out of nowhere,” The New York Times wrote, tactfully. Our girl Alice is also an alleged honeypot who was recruited by the Chinese Ministry of State Security. (China is denying all this, btw.) What is Megaspeed? Well. The company has ties to the Chinese military and builds data centers in “Southeast Asia” (it has offices in Singapore and Indonesia) to sell compute to Alibaba. The chips it is using to do that are banned from being imported to China. Incidentally, Nvidia has been lobbying very intensely to get rid of import controls on its chips so it can sell them in China. This is all public knowledge in part because Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly “oversaw” a memo detailing Alice’s recruitment and relationship with Jensen, and then someone leaked it. (Powerful memo game, Marco, getting credit for one you didn’t even write!) Rubio passed his little note around in May, ahead of a trip to China taken by President Donald Trump. Jensen initially didn’t make the list of invitees on the trip — at least, not until Trump saw media coverage of the perceived snub. Trump and Jensen? They’re close. Which makes it even more interesting that Trump was personally briefed on the findings and did nothing, according to the Times. You know shit is going good when your corporate spokesperson has to tell the Times that of course your company does not disclose classified information to your customers. John Rizzo, the spokesman, also told the Times that Nvidia’s customers don’t ask Nvidia to lobby for changes to the chip restriction. Bit of a hat on a hat, John. First of all, they don’t have to — Nvidia’s financial incentives do it for them. Second, imagine this is a regular company. The business model of Megaspeed is that the chips are restricted, and that Megaspeed gets ahold of them. Megaspeed has no incentive to upend this situation! Unless, you know, it’s acting against its financial interest because it’s a front for Chinese spies… in which case, that statement is going to be embarrassing. Speaking of embarrassing, Rizzo told the Times “that Mr. Huang’s interactions with Ms. Huang were ‘not unusual’ and consistent with the kinds of meetings he has with any of Nvidia’s many customers.” Oh, okay. Who else was Jensen fucking? Because two days after that statement, Jensen sent the most incredible email addressed “To my colleagues at Nvidia” in which he admitted he had been “unfaithful.” Then, he wrote, “To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.” Are… your wife and family on the Nvidia employee email list? Well, yes! His son is a director of product management; his daughter is a senior marketing director. He even gave a job to his son-in-law! Also, Nvidia has an extraordinary structure. Jensen has 60 direct reports. Leave aside that there is no possible way to manage that many people well. I would like to direct your attention to something else entirely: If he is in trouble, there is no part of the company that is untouched. The usual problems attain, of course — he was in a position to have gotten any information she might have requested! He could have left company laptops available for infiltration! But because of the structure, he also could have issued commands to his many direct reports that benefited the CCP. Neat! I sure hope someone who knows a lot about cybersecurity is going through Nvidia with a fine-toothed comb. Is he in trouble? Well, Nvidia is opening an investigation into Jensen, who is also its largest individual shareholder. (At least there’s no dual-class stock!) Nvidia shares are, as of this writing, down almost five percent, which seems like an underreaction. Perhaps more consequentially, the Democratic Party just swept back into power and Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) seems mad. Also, the voters hate the data centers that house Nvidia chips, and I notice a lot of ambitious politicians thinking about the next presidential elections. For instance, there’s Rubio’s name attached to the memo. I also notice Trump’s popularity is at an all-time nadir. Besides any Democrats positioning themselves for a run, a Republican looking to create some daylight between himself and Trump could easily do so by going to town on Jensen, who is Trump’s buddy. I do not think Rubio is the only ambition monster to worry about. I don’t know where Jensen’s actual wife, Lori, is in all this. They got married in 1985. She gave up her job as a microchip designer to raise their kids. I would be very surprised if there is a prenup. I would be somewhat surprised if there was a postnup. Jensen doesn’t own as much of Nvidia as Jeff Bezos did of Amazon when he cheated on and divorced his wife, but it’s something to keep an eye on, if Lori decides she’s out. We’ve talked once or twice about Nvidia’s central role in the AI ecosystem — and specifically, that it is heavily involved in financing AI neoclouds. It has investments in SpaceX, CoreWeave (where it was, as of the time of the IPO, the company’s second-biggest customer), and OpenAI, among others. Jensen has been promoting “compute as an asset class.” One of the reasons I have been uncertain about when and how the AI bubble will pop is that it seems to me that Nvidia can bail out any or all of these companies anytime it needs to, just like it did for CoreWeave when its IPO was threatened. Neoclouds exist because Nvidia wanted to create competition for its chips, so its biggest customers — Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Oracle — couldn’t exert too much pricing pressure. Certainly I am not the only person who has noticed that Nvidia is, effectively, the central bank of AI. If Nvidia is in a particularly bad way, it kind of seems like, at minimum, the neoclouds get fucked too. Oddly, CoreWeave is up about 6 percent as of this writing; the stock market moves in mysterious ways. Maybe that is why our nation’s foremost thought leaders on X are posting things like “Whomst among us hasn’t accidentally fucked a Chinese spy? That’s how it is on this bitch of an earth.” I’m kidding, here’s investor/loudmouth Bill Ackman: “We should all support him and his family. Onward.” Shaun Maguire, partner at VC firm Sequoia: “I believe Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership.” (Elon Musk took a quick break from complaining about Dave Chappelle’s comedy to type “I agree” to Maguire’s note.) So Jensen can’t go down, as there’s no one who can replace him, and Nvidia can’t go down, as nothing can replace it. The AI industry better hope there isn’t some further revelation coming that would make one of these things unavoidable, such as the investigation finding proof that Alice directly accessed Nvidia’s systems while Jensen was showering or something. Might also be bad if, say, a US Commerce Department inquiry into Megaspeed was halted after Nvidia intervened. Didn’t we just hear somewhere that Jensen had been influencing the Trump administration’s policy on export controls? Anyway, as of this note, Jensen isn’t planning to step down as CEO. Might as well settle in for the most fun we’ll have until we find out that Musk did IVF with a family member of Chinese President Xi Jinping.

articles.title: Meta releases Muse Ember, a new lightweight model for agent execution | TechCrunch
articles.summary: At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna.
articles.body:
Meta Superintelligence Lab released a new AI model on Monday called Muse Ember, the lab’s lightest and most cost-efficient AI model yet. In its release, Meta said Ember was “designed for complex reasoning execution and the work agents repeat all day: tool calls, coding subtasks, routing, extraction, and long document parsing.”

Meta particularly emphasized Ember’s cost-per-task, using Artificial Analysis’s composite benchmark score to show Ember as cheaper and smarter than competitors like Anthropic’s Haiku and OpenAI’s Luna.

At 10 cents per million input tokens, Ember is significantly cheaper than frontier competitors like Haiku and Luna. Not only that, it’s cost-competitive with open source competitors like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 Flash.

Given the emphasis on low cost and accuracy at scale, Ember is designed to pair with a larger model like Meta’s Muse Wonder in an agentic harness. In the case of a customer-support agent, for instance, you might see a heavier model establishing rules for how to handle a particular issue, then sending a lighter-weight model to apply the rules across tens of thousands of cases. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “Muse Wonder plans, Muse Ember handles the volume.”

With volume-heavy use cases in mind, Meta also trained Ember to work well across different types of media, including text, images, and audio. The result makes the model surprisingly flexible in what kind of inputs it can handle. As Meta puts it in the announcement, “agents can read screenshots, charts, and scanned documents, or work from voice memos, meeting recordings, and video without a separate model.”

Ember is the fourth model released under Meta’s Muse brand, following the mid-weight Spark ( released in April ), Spark’s open source twin Glimmer ( released in August ), and the Wonder frontier model ( released in October ). The flagship consumer AI product, the Muse Agent, was released in September to unexpected success , with new features like Spaces and video chat rolling out earlier this month.

articles.title: Anthropic launches new Claude Fable and Mythos 5.2 models

articles.body: Anthropic is announcing two new models today: Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, which it says are designed to take on “daunting” technical challenges. The company claims the new models show improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision, and can generate outputs faster than the 5.1 versions of the Fable and Mythos models. Claude Fable 5.2 is good at challenging software engineering problems, Anthropic says, and can orchestrate agent teams and tackle long-running projects. The new model has also solved some complex scientific problems, including two open theoretical physics problems. During prerelease testing, the two models have “helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours,” Anthropic says.
